title: In half a day, the Bay of Fundy's tide moves twice the flow of all Earth's rivers
body: Canada's Bay of Fundy, between New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, has the highest tidal range in the world, about **16 m** between low and high water, where the average worldwide is only about 1 m. In one half-day tidal cycle, around 100 billion tonnes of water flows in and out of the bay. The cause is tidal resonance: the bay's long funnel shape makes its water slosh back and forth in step with the tides, so each push builds on the last, like a swing pushed at just the right moment.

slides.heading: Tidal range: the world's average versus Fundy
slides.note: Average tidal range worldwide is only about 1 m; in the Bay of Fundy it is about 16 m

slides.alt: The same Hopewell Rocks sea stacks at low tide, standing on a wide muddy sea floor where visitors are walking
slides.caption: The same rocks at low tide. Visitors walk on the sea floor around stacks that stand in water at high tide.

slides.label: the highest water level ever recorded in the bay
slides.text: In October 1869 the Saxby Gale's storm surge struck at the same time as an especially strong spring tide.

slides.prompt: The incoming tide pushes a wave called a tidal bore up the Petitcodiac River. In 2013, how far did surfers ride it?
slides.detail: Before a causeway was built in 1968, the bore reached up to 2 m high. It returned after the causeway gates were opened in 2010.

slides.question: Why are the tides in the Bay of Fundy so huge?
options: Its water sloshes in step with the tide
The Moon passes closer to it
slides.explanation: This tidal resonance in the bay's funnel-shaped basin makes each tide build on the last, like pushes on a swing.
